month.title: AI engineering
month.theme: Treat model output as uncertain software behaviour, and build features that are useful, measurable and under human control.
month.mastery: Build an AI feature with structured output and basic evaluation.
month.checkpoint: An AI feature with server-side model calls, validated structured output, a 20-case evaluation set and a review/edit flow.

weeks.title: LLM fundamentals
weeks.objective: Understand what a language model actually does, so you can predict where it will help and where it will fail.
learn: Models predict tokens, and what that implies
Tokens, context windows and cost
Temperature and sampling
Training data, knowledge cutoffs, and why models 'hallucinate'
System prompts, user messages and roles
Model trade-offs: capability vs latency vs cost
Open vs closed models; running locally vs via an API
practice: Count tokens for the same paragraph in two different tokenizers
Ask the same question five times at a low and at a high temperature; compare
Find three questions a model answers confidently and wrongly
Run the same task in two different providers' playgrounds

build.title: Model field notes
build.brief: A small comparison page: one realistic design-studio task (for example turning a client brief into a project scope) run across 2–3 models, with notes on quality, latency, cost and failure modes.

weeks.prove: Explain to a non-technical colleague why the model 'made something up', and what you'd do about it in a product.
reflect: What did you believe about LLMs at the start of the week that turned out to be wrong?

tryFirst.task: Estimate the cost of summarising 1,000 client briefs of about 1,500 words each into 150-word summaries.
tryFirst.hint: Roughly, 1 token ≈ 0.75 English words. Input and output are priced separately per million tokens. Look up a current price for one model.
tryFirst.explanation: Cost = input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price. Doing this arithmetic before building tells you whether a feature is viable, which model tier to use, and whether to cache or batch.
tryFirst.solution:
Input:  1,500 words ≈ 2,000 tokens × 1,000 = 2,000,000 tokens
Output:   150 words ≈   200 tokens × 1,000 =   200,000 tokens

At an example price of $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens:
2 × $1 + 0.2 × $5 = $3.00 for the whole batch

(Prices change. Always check the provider's current pricing page.)

weeks.title: Model APIs
weeks.objective: Call models from your own server safely, with cost, latency and failures under control.
learn: API keys, server-side calls, environment variables
Request structure: model, messages, max tokens
Streaming responses
Errors: rate limits, timeouts, overloaded models
Retries with backoff
Cost guards: input caps, output caps, usage logging
Hiding the provider behind your own interface so you can switch
practice: Make a first API call from a script with two different providers
Stream a response into a page
Handle a forced error (bad key, tiny max tokens)
Log tokens used and cost per call

build.title: 'Summarise this brief' endpoint
build.brief: Add a server-side endpoint to one of your apps that summarises pasted text. The key stays on the server, input length is capped, the UI shows loading or streaming, errors are clear, and usage is logged.

weeks.prove: Show that the key never reaches the browser, and that a 50,000-word paste is rejected before it costs you money.
reflect: Where would this feature break at 100× the users?
weeks.ship: Deployed endpoint, with a README section on cost and limits.

tryFirst.task: Write a provider-agnostic function your app calls to summarise text, so that switching model providers later touches one file.
tryFirst.hint: Your app shouldn't know which company's SDK sits underneath. Define the input and output you need, and hide the provider behind that.
tryFirst.explanation: An adapter (a thin interface around the provider) keeps vendor details in one place. It also centralises the guards (input caps, timeouts, logging) so every call gets them.

weeks.title: Prompting and structured outputs
weeks.objective: Get reliable, machine-readable output from a model, and never trust it without validating it.
learn: Clear task framing, context and examples (few-shot)
System prompts and roles
Structured output: JSON schemas and tool-based output
Validating model output with a schema
Handling refusals, partial output and malformed output
Versioning prompts
When a plain deterministic function beats a model
practice: Write the same prompt three ways (vague, specific, with examples) and compare
Ask for JSON matching a schema and validate it with Zod
Feed it inputs designed to break the format
Keep your prompts in versioned files, not inline strings

build.title: Brief-to-scope extractor
build.brief: Paste a messy client brief and get back validated JSON (deliverables, deadlines, budget signals, open questions, risks), shown as an editable form.

weeks.prove: Run 15 varied briefs through it. Record how many produce valid, correct output, and categorise the failures.
reflect: Which failures were the model's fault, and which were your prompt's?
weeks.ship: Extractor deployed, with a prompts/ folder and a failures table in the README.

tryFirst.task: Your model returns JSON most of the time, but sometimes adds commentary or misses fields. Make the feature safe.
tryFirst.hint: Two layers: ask for structure in the way the API supports best, then check what came back before using it.
tryFirst.explanation: Use the provider's structured-output or tool mechanism where available, then validate with a schema anyway. On failure, retry once; if it still fails, show a recoverable state. Never render unvalidated output.

weeks.title: AI product UX + evaluation
weeks.objective: Design AI features people can trust, and measure whether they work before you polish them.
learn: Human control: review, edit, accept, undo
Showing uncertainty and sources
Latency UX: streaming, skeletons, progress
Evaluation sets: representative inputs and expected outcomes
Rubrics and simple scoring
Regression-testing prompts
Collecting user feedback in the product
practice: Write 20 test cases for your extractor, including nasty edge cases
Score two prompt versions against the same set
Design the review/edit flow in Figma first
Add thumbs up/down with a reason

build.title: Extractor with review flow + eval set
build.brief: Add a review/edit/accept flow to your extractor, and a repeatable evaluation script over 20 cases with a simple scoreboard.

weeks.prove: Mastery test: build an AI feature with structured output and basic evaluation.
reflect: What did evaluation reveal that demo-testing never would have?
weeks.ship: Deployed AI feature, with an evaluation results table in the README.

tryFirst.task: Design a tiny evaluation for your brief extractor that you can re-run after every prompt change.
tryFirst.hint: Fix a set of inputs. For each one, decide what 'correct' means in checkable terms. Count; don't go on vibes.
tryFirst.explanation: An eval is a test suite for behaviour: fixed cases, explicit checks, and a score you can compare across versions. Start with simple automated checks (fields present, known deadline found) plus a human-scored rubric.

mastery.title: AI feature with structured output and evaluation
mastery.challenge: Ship an AI feature that does one real job for a user (from your own work or a problem in your Opportunity Lab), returns validated structured output, and is measured by an evaluation set.
constraints: Model calls only from the server; no keys in the browser
The provider is hidden behind your own adapter
AI coding help is allowed, but you must pass the ownership check
criteria: Output is validated against a schema before display, and invalid output is handled
At least 20 evaluation cases with a recorded score
Two prompt or model versions compared with numbers
The user can review, edit or reject output before it's saved
Cost per use estimated and capped
You can explain every file that touches the model
